passage:
"Leela, it's your special time now. Just you and me. What shall we do?"
"Can we read the elephant book? Only us?"
"Only us. Seema is with Appa."
After ten minutes, Amma called, "Seema, your turn!"
"Amma, can we do puzzle?"
"Yes, kanna."
Later, Amma put a big cardboard box on the floor. "Can you two make a house together?"
"I'll do the door!" said Leela.
"I'll do windows!" said Seema.
"Help me hold this, Seema!"
"Okay, akka!"
Amma smiled. They didn't fight once.

qa.q: What did Leela want to read in her special time?
qa.a: She wanted to read the elephant book, just with Amma.

qa.q: How can you tell Leela was happy about her special time?
qa.a: She asked "Only us?" eagerly, showing she loved having Amma to herself.

qa.q: Why does the cardboard house work well after special time?
qa.a: Each child already feels sure of Amma's attention, so building together feels fun and they help each other instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might Seema feel helping her akka build the house?
qa.a: She likely feels proud and happy to be working with Leela. 😊

grounding: It shows each child getting a short time alone with the parent and then building something together, which eases rivalry.

Note on the fridge, from Manjula, for Appa.
Week two of our plan: 10 minutes alone with each child every evening. Devika (6) chose to paint with me. Kartik (4) chose rolling a ball. Both waited their turn without fighting.
Today they built a train from shoe boxes together. Devika held the tape, Kartik stuck on wheels. Kartik said, "Akka, we're a team!" Devika laughed.
Fewer fights this week. 🎉

qa.q: What did Kartik choose to do in his time alone?
qa.a: Kartik chose rolling a ball.

qa.q: What does Kartik's "Akka, we're a team!" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he feels happy and proud working with his sister, and enjoys being on her side.

qa.q: Why might the plan be reducing fights?
qa.a: Each child gets reliable time alone, so they feel sure of their place, and building the train shows them that working together feels good.

qa.q: How might Devika see her little brother now?
qa.a: She may see Kartik more as a teammate than a rival, laughing with him as they build.

grounding: It illustrates each child getting short daily time alone with a parent and building something together, easing rivalry through security and cooperation.

Every evening, in their village near Nashik, Amma gave Sumit ten minutes alone. They walked to the well and back, and he told her about frogs and the new calf.

Then Bhavna got ten minutes, braiding Amma's hair on the step.

On Sundays they had one job together: a mud house for the clay dolls by the tulsi plant. Sumit found sticks; Bhavna made the door.

After two weeks, the fighting was less. Sumit didn't knock Bhavna's things over anymore. He was too busy building.

qa.q: Where did Amma and Sumit walk each evening?
qa.a: To the well and back.

qa.q: How do Sumit and Bhavna seem to feel after two weeks of their special time?
qa.a: They seem more secure and content, sure of their own place with Amma, so they fight less.

qa.q: Why does building the mud house together help?
qa.a: It gives the siblings a shared goal, so they discover cooperating feels good, instead of competing.

qa.q: How might Amma feel seeing Sumit busy building instead of fighting?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved and pleased that her plan is working.

grounding: Amma gives Sumit and Bhavna each a short daily time alone and a shared building task, and their rivalry eases as each feels sure of their place.

subtype: Stage 6: One-on-one time and joint tasks [Response]
passage:
In Berlin, Selin and Abebe had fought every day since their baby sister was born.

So their mother made a plan. Every evening after dinner, Selin got fifteen minutes with Mama alone, reading picture books on the big chair. Then Abebe got fifteen minutes, building train tracks on the floor.

On Saturdays they made pancakes together. Selin cracked eggs; Abebe stirred.

By the third Saturday, when Abebe dropped an egg, Selin said, "It's okay, I'll get another one," instead of shouting.

Mama watched them and smiled.

qa.q: What did Selin and Abebe make together on Saturdays?
qa.a: Pancakes.

qa.q: What does Selin's kind reply about the egg show?
qa.a: It shows she feels more secure and warmer towards Abebe, enjoying cooperation instead of competing.

qa.q: How does Mama's plan ease the rivalry?
qa.a: Each child gets time alone with her, so they feel sure of their place, and a joint task shows them cooperation feels good.

qa.q: How might Abebe feel when Selin says "It's okay"?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy, expecting a scolding but getting kindness.

grounding: Mama gives Selin and Abebe short daily one-on-one times and a shared pancake job, and rivalry eases as each feels sure of their place.

subtype: Stage 6: One-on-one time and joint tasks [Response]
passage:
In the Mumbai child clinic's waiting room, Lalit and his little sister Tia built a foam tower, taking turns. A month ago, they'd have been hitting each other.

Inside, their mother Devika told the counsellor, "I did what you suggested. Ten minutes a day with each of them, alone. Lalit and I play cars. Tia and I sing. And every evening they have one job together, watering the plants."

"Fewer fights now. Lalit told me yesterday, 'Mumma, tomorrow is my car time, right?' Like he's sure it's coming."

The counsellor nodded. Through the glass, Lalit was helping Tia put the last block on top.

qa.q: What job do Lalit and Tia do together every evening?
qa.a: Watering the plants.

qa.q: What does Lalit's question about car time suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels secure and sure of his own time with Mumma, which eases his need to compete.

qa.q: Why did Devika's plan work?
qa.a: Daily one-on-one time made each child sure of their place, and a joint task showed them cooperation feels good.

qa.q: What might Tia's singing time with Mumma mean to her?
qa.a: It probably makes Tia feel special and secure, so she has less need to fight Lalit for attention.

grounding: At a clinic Devika reports that daily one-on-one time and a shared task have eased her children's rivalry, as each feels sure of their place.
